section.title: Walk in Love and Truth
section.sectionRationale: From the greeting the elder turns to his first appeal. Overjoyed to find some of the children walking in the truth, he urges the old commandment to love one another, and then defines that love as walking in obedience to God. This is the positive heart of the letter, before the warning that follows.
section.thesis: The elder rejoices to see God's people walking in the truth, and he presses on them the commandment they have had from the beginning, to love one another, defining that love as walking according to God's commandments.
section.frameNote: Three beats: joy at children walking in truth; the old commandment to love; love defined as obedient walking.

verses.text: I was overjoyed to find some of your children {{peripateo|walking}} in the {{aletheia|truth}}, just as the Father has commanded us.
And now I urge you, dear lady, not as a new commandment to you, but one we have had from the beginning, that we {{agape|love}} one another.
And this is love, that we walk according to His {{entole|commandments}}. This is the very commandment you have heard from the beginning, that you must walk in love.

peripateo.gloss: To walk, and figuratively to conduct one's whole life. John loves this image: faith is a way of walking, a daily path rather than a mere feeling. To walk in the truth is to let the reality of God in Christ shape one's actual living, step by step.

aletheia.gloss: Truth, reality, what is genuine. Here it is something one walks in, a path lived out, not only a creed believed. The elder's joy is that the children are not merely holding right ideas but ordering their lives by the truth of God revealed in Christ.

agape.gloss: Love, self-giving devotion that seeks another's good. This is the commandment the elder presses, to love one another, and it is the same command God's people have had from the beginning. In this letter love is inseparable from truth and from obedience.

entole.gloss: Commandment, an authoritative charge. John uses it for God's directives, above all the command to love. Strikingly, love itself is defined by walking according to His commandments, so love and obedience are bound together and interpret one another.

basic.context: Having greeted his readers, the elder now makes his first appeal. He is thrilled to have found some of the lady's children living by the truth. On that happy note he urges the command they have always known: love one another. Then he explains what that love actually is, walking in obedience to God.
basic.hermeneutics: The elder deliberately calls the command to love both old and familiar, not a novelty. He also refuses to let love float free of obedience: love is defined as walking according to God's commandments, and the commandment is to walk in love. The two are locked together on purpose.
basic.originalLanguages: Walking, peripateo, is John's picture of the whole Christian life, a daily path. The children walk in the truth, aletheia, and are urged to love, agape, one another. And love is measured by walking according to His commandments, entole, so love and obedience define each other.
basic.typology: There is no formal type here, but the pattern reaches back and forward: the command from the beginning echoes the law of love God always intended for His people, and it is fulfilled and deepened in Jesus, who made loving one another the mark of His disciples.
basic.christ: The command to love one another is the very command Jesus gave His disciples, calling it new in the sense that His own self-giving love became its pattern. To walk in love as Jesus commanded is to walk after Him, and He is the one whose obedience and love were perfectly one.
basic.god: God is a Father who commands, and what He commands is love. He does not set truth and love against each other, nor love and obedience; He binds them together. To obey God and to love one another are, in His design, the same path.
basic.crossReferences: John 13 is where Jesus gives the new commandment to love one another. 1 John repeatedly ties love to obedience and to walking in the light. Together they show that real love keeps God's word.
basic.oneStory: God has always called His people to love, and here that ancient command is pressed again, now shaped by Christ. Love that keeps God's commandments and obedience that expresses love are one path, the way God's redeemed people are meant to walk until the end.

context.literary:
Verses 4 to 6 form one tightly woven unit, and the weave is made of repeated words. 'Commandment' occurs four times in three verses, in verses 4, 5 and 6 twice. The verb 'walk' opens the unit in verse 4 and closes it in verse 6, so that the little paragraph begins and ends on the same word, a framing device scholars call an inclusio. 'Love' is introduced by the request in verse 5, defined in verse 6, and returned to as the sphere of the walking in the last clause. And 'from the beginning' appears at the centre, binding the first command to the oldest authority the readers know.

The logic is circular on purpose. Verse 6 says, first, that love means walking according to His commandments, and second, that the commandment is that you walk in love. Love is defined by obedience, and obedience by love. Neither is allowed to stand alone. Anyone who tries to keep God's commands coldly, or to love warmly without regard to what God has said, has broken the circle.

Observe the sequence of speech acts. The letter moves from the elder's own emotion, 'I was overjoyed,' to a polite request, 'I urge you, dear lady,' to a flat statement, 'this is love.' It is a small ladder from feeling to appeal to definition. Notice also the quiet 'some' in verse 4. Not all the children were found walking in the truth, or at least not all were found. The warm tone of the paragraph is already holding a worry that the warning of verses 7 to 11 will bring out into the open.
context.historical:
The elder had met some of the lady's children. In the first century such meetings usually happened because believers travelled, for trade, for family, or for the sake of the churches, and the network of house congregations kept one another informed by visits and by short letters like this one. His 'finding' them walking in the truth suggests he saw their way of life at first hand and not merely heard a report. Early Christians were not defined chiefly by buildings or by official membership lists, but by the shape of their lives, and a visitor could learn a great deal by seeing how a family spent its days.

The request to 'love one another' had a particular edge in the late first century. Congregations were being tested from outside by suspicion and occasional persecution, and from inside by teachers who had left the apostolic circle, 1 John 2:19, and were pulling believers after them. In such a season the temptation was either to turn hard against the dissenters or to dissolve the church's boundaries in the name of love. The elder is steering between the two.

The command itself was already old when John wrote. Jesus had given it to His disciples on the night before His death, John 13:34, perhaps sixty years earlier, and it rested on the Law, where loving one's neighbour is commanded in Leviticus 19:18 and loving God in Deuteronomy 6:5. When the elder says 'from the beginning,' the first hearers could take it to mean from the beginning of their own Christian life, from the start of the gospel's preaching, or from the beginning of Jesus' ministry. Each of these ancient horizons was available to them, and all of them were true.
context.canonical:
The paragraph takes up the upper room. In John 13:34-35 Jesus calls love for one another 'a new commandment,' and in John 15:12 He repeats it as His own commandment, adding the standard, 'as I have loved you.' In John 14:15 and 21 and 15:10 He ties love for Himself to keeping His commands. The elder, who had heard these words, folds them into a single pastoral sentence in verse 6.

The first letter works out the same ideas at greater length. In 1 John 2:7-8 the same writer calls the command both old and new, in the same breath, and 1 John 3:11 reminds the readers that the message they heard from the beginning is that they should love one another. First John 5:3 states what verse 6 here already hints, that to love God is to keep His commandments, and that those commandments are not burdensome. Third John 3-4 voices the same joy as verse 4, saying that he has no greater joy than to hear that his children are walking in the truth.

Beyond John, the paragraph belongs to a larger biblical pattern. Paul tells the Ephesians to 'walk in love, just as Christ loved us,' Ephesians 5:2, and says in Romans 13:8-10 that love fulfils the law. James speaks of the royal law, 'Love your neighbor as yourself,' James 2:8. The Old Testament's language of walking in God's ways, Deuteronomy 10:12, and walking in His truth, Psalm 86:11, is the soil in which the Johannine phrase grew.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The elder wants to affirm what is going well before he addresses what is not. His joy is sincere, and it also performs a task: it tells the readers that he sees them as people already walking in the truth, so that what follows is correction among friends. He is not suspicious of the household. He is guarding something he believes is valuable and already present.

His appeal is simple and deliberately unoriginal. He does not offer a new programme or a fresh insight. He urges the oldest command they know, and he says so. For the first readers this was an intentional safeguard against teachers who claimed to bring something more advanced. The elder's answer is that real progress is not beyond love but deeper into it.

He also intends to prevent a misreading. Love can be turned into a feeling, a mood or a refusal to disagree. By saying that love is walking according to God's commandments, he fixes it to what God has actually said and to what people actually do. The readers were meant to leave the paragraph unable to separate affection from obedience, and unable to claim one without the other. The same sentence that urges them to love also gives them a way to test whether they are doing so.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verse 4 is description: the elder reports what he found and how he felt. It should not be turned into a rule that a teacher must always be overjoyed, or that every family will be found walking in the truth. What it does give is a pattern for pastoral affection, the habit of noticing and naming what God is doing in people.

Verses 5 and 6 are prescription. The request to love one another is addressed to the readers, and the definition of love as walking according to His commandments applies to every believer in every age. The text does not tell us to adopt a list of rules as the content of love. It tells us that love will take the shape of obedience to what God has said, and the same person who loves will want to know what God commands. Both the sphere and the pattern are fixed: love, and love that obeys.

One caution belongs here. To define love as obedience does not mean that obedience earns God's love or that love is only a matter of rule keeping. The love in view is love that responds to the Father who first loved us, 1 John 4:19, and obedience is its fruit and not its price.

debates.question: What does 'from the beginning' mean in verses 5 and 6?

views.label: From the start of the readers' Christian life
views.case: In 1 John 2:24 the readers are told to let what they heard from the beginning remain in them, and in 1 John 3:11 the message heard 'from the beginning' is that they should love one another. On this reading the beginning is the point at which the gospel first reached them. The command is old because they have always been taught it.

views.label: From the beginning of Jesus' ministry and the apostles' witness
views.case: John uses 'from the beginning' of the eyewitness testimony in 1 John 1:1 and of the time the disciples have been with Jesus, John 15:27. The command is then the one given in the upper room, delivered by the Lord Himself, and is the oldest Christian authority possible.

views.label: From the beginning of God's dealings with His people
views.case: The love command is already present in the Law, Leviticus 19:18 and Deuteronomy 6:5, and some take 'from the beginning' to reach back to the Old Testament, so that the command is as old as the covenant. The phrase would then link Jesus' new command to the ancient demand.

debates.bearing: All three are defensible and none excludes the others, which suggests the phrase is deliberately wide. What matters for the paragraph is the contrast with novelty: whatever the exact date, the command to love is not a recent invention and so cannot be improved upon by a newer teaching.

debates.question: Does 'some of your children' imply that other children were not walking in the truth?

views.label: It reports only the ones he met
views.case: The elder had not met the whole household. He rejoices over the ones he found, and the phrase says nothing about the rest. Reading criticism into the word 'some' is reading too much into ordinary speech.

views.label: It quietly hints at trouble
views.case: A writer who was fully content would have said 'your children.' The careful 'some' fits a letter that moves on to warn about deceivers and about those who run ahead, and it may reflect the knowledge that part of the family or congregation had gone another way.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle the question. The right response is to take the joy at face value and to remember that the next verses show why the elder cannot afford to be careless about those who are not walking in the truth.

study.originalLanguages:
The joy of verse 4 is carefully worded. 'I was overjoyed' is a form of the verb chairo with the adverb lian, 'greatly,' and the matching line in 3 John 4 uses the noun chara, 'I have no greater joy.' The reason for the joy is expressed with a perfect tense verb, 'I have found,' heureka, meaning a discovery whose result stands. The elder is not remembering a distant day; he is reporting what is now settled in his mind.

The children are found 'walking,' peripatountas, in the present tense. A present participle describes a continuing habit, not a single act. It is exactly what 3 John 3 means by 'in which you continue to walk.' The verb itself is literally 'walk around,' and the Bible uses it for the whole course of life. In the Old Testament the equivalent Hebrew verb halak is used of walking with God, as with Enoch in Genesis 5:24, and of keeping His ways, Deuteronomy 10:12. The phrase 'walk in your truth' appears in Psalm 86:11.

The commandment of verse 4 'we received from the Father' is in the aorist, a completed past act, which points back to the moment of giving. In verse 5 the word translated 'new' is kainos, which means new in kind or quality, not neos, which means new in time. John is not saying the command is recent but that it is fresh with a new standard, which 1 John 2:7-8 handles by saying that it is old and also new. The verb that carries the request, erotao, is a word of asking or requesting and not of command. The elder pleads with the lady as a brother and does not issue an order.

The content of the request is introduced by hina with a present subjunctive, 'that we love,' agapomen. The present tense means keep on loving, as a continuing practice, and 'one another' is allelous, the reciprocal pronoun, which makes the love mutual and not merely directed from the strong to the weak.

Verse 6 turns on a small ambiguity. 'The very commandment you have heard from the beginning, that you must walk in love,' ends with the Greek en aute, literally 'in her' or 'in it.' The feminine pronoun can point back to love, agape, or to the commandment, entole, both of which are feminine nouns. Either way the sense is close, since to walk in the commandment is to walk in love. Notice too that 'commandments' is plural in the first half of the verse and the commandment is singular in the second, as though the many commands are gathered up in the one.

typology.type: The command to love, from Sinai to the upper room
typology.fulfillment: The Law said, 'Love your neighbor as yourself,' Leviticus 19:18, and Jesus placed it beside love for God as the two greatest commandments, Mark 12:29-31. Paul says that love is the fulfilment of the law, Romans 13:10. The elder's 'from the beginning' stands in this line, and the standard rises in Christ: not as yourself but 'as I have loved you,' John 13:34. The earlier command was written on stone and measured by self-love; the new covenant writes it on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33, and measures it by the cross. The type falls short in that the Law could command love but could not supply it.

typology.type: Walking with God, from Enoch to the Spirit
typology.fulfillment: Enoch walked with God, Genesis 5:24, and Israel was told to walk in all His ways, Deuteronomy 10:12. The pattern is of life lived in company with God, step by step. In Christ the walk becomes possible for all: God sent His Son so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in those who walk according to the Spirit, Romans 8:3-4, and Ezekiel 36:27 promised that God would cause His people to walk in His statutes. The type falls short because Enoch and the faithful of old walked by promise, while believers now walk by the Spirit who dwells within them.

Throughout John, the Son does what the Father commands, John 12:49-50, and He tells His disciples that they will remain in His love if they keep His commandments, just as He has kept His Father's commandments and remains in His love, John 15:10. The elder's definition of love as obedient walking is a copy of the pattern in the Son, who humbled Himself and became obedient to death, Philippians 2:8. The correspondence is real, but it does not run both ways: the disciples copy Christ's obedience, while only Christ's obedience can bear sin.

study.christ:
The paragraph leads to Christ by the command that He gave. When the elder says 'we love one another,' he is quoting the Lord. In the upper room Jesus called it 'a new commandment,' John 13:34, and the newness lay in the measure, 'As I have loved you.' It was about to be displayed on a cross. The elder's phrase 'from the beginning' therefore need not reach into the dusty past. It can mean from the beginning of the gospel, from the night in which Jesus said it, and the readers had never known a time when they were allowed to leave it behind.

It leads to Christ by the shape of obedience. The elder says that love is walking according to His commandments, and the 'His' can be read as the Father's or the Son's. In John both are true. Jesus says that if we love Him we will keep His commandments, John 14:15, and also that the Father gave Him the command about what to say, John 12:49-50. The commands are the Father's and the Son's together, because Father and Son act as one. To walk in obedience to them is to walk after Jesus, who said 'I am the way and the truth and the life,' John 14:6. In a very real sense, walking in the truth is following the One who is the truth, and the first letter says it plainly: whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus walked, 1 John 2:6.

It leads to Christ by contrast with false teachers. The deceivers of the next paragraph offer something supposedly more advanced. The elder holds the readers to the old command because Christ has given nothing greater and nothing different. Love is not an elementary lesson that advanced believers leave behind. It is the content of the whole discipleship.

And it leads to Christ by supply. The elder does not say how the readers can love as Christ loved, but the rest of the New Testament does. Paul says that the righteous standard of the law is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit, Romans 8:4, and that we love because He first loved us, 1 John 4:19. The One who commands love is the One who provides it. It would be a misreading to treat the verse as only a moral standard. It is first a description of life with a Saviour who has done what the commandment demands and who now works it out in His people.
study.god:
Verse 4 shows God as a Father who commands. The sentence says that the elder found the children walking in the truth 'just as the Father has commanded us.' God's commands are not the orders of a distant authority but the instructions of a Father to children he loves. That makes all the difference to how they are received. The same letter says that His commandments are not burdensome, 1 John 5:3, because they come from one who loved first, 1 John 4:19.

He is a God whose commands are consistent. The command to love is not changed from age to age. It is the same in Leviticus 19:18, in the upper room, and in the elder's pastoral note. This consistency shows an unchanging character, a God who does not have one moral will for the old covenant and a different one for the new. What changes is how it is done, not what is asked. In the old covenant the command was written on tablets, and in the new it is written on hearts, Jeremiah 31:33.

He is a God who joins things that people want to separate. The elder's circle of love and obedience is God's own design. He does not command truth apart from love or love apart from truth, and He does not allow the church to imagine that affection can replace His word or that His word can be kept without affection. The unity of His commandments reflects the unity of His own character, which is both holy and loving.

He is a God who delights in the walking of His people. The elder is overjoyed, and his joy is a pale reflection of the Father's, who rejoices over His people with singing, Zephaniah 3:17. The idea that God is mainly displeased with His children is not found here. What delights the Father is a household that walks in truth.

For worship, the paragraph invites believers to ask what God has actually said and then to do it in love. It also reminds them that they do not bring this obedience to God as a payment but as a response. They walk because they have been loved, and the Father who commanded them is the same Father who gave His Son so that they might.

crossReferences.note: The upper room command is the immediate source of verse 5. Jesus calls it new because the standard is now His own love, and He says that the world will know His disciples by it. The elder's urging is simply this word handed down to the next generation.

The first letter describes the same command as both old and new, one the readers have had from the beginning, and shows that its newness lies in the light that is now shining. It explains why verse 5 can speak of an old command and yet press it as fresh.

John says that the love of God is to keep His commandments and that they are not burdensome. It is the plainest statement of the circle of verse 6, and shows that obedience is the expression of love, not a weight laid upon it.

The elder says he has no greater joy than to hear that his children are walking in the truth. It is the same joy as verse 4, repeated in the companion letter, and shows that the sight of faithful walking was the thing that most moved him.

Jesus ties love for Him to keeping His commands, and promises that the Father and He will love and make their home with the one who obeys. It stands behind the definition of love as obedience and shows that obedience opens the way into fellowship with God.

The Lord says that His disciples will remain in His love if they keep His commands, as He has kept His Father's, and gives the command to love as He has loved. The passage shows the pattern in the Son that the elder asks the church to copy.

Paul tells believers to walk in love as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us. It uses the same verb and the same image as verse 6 and shows that the Johannine phrase was part of a wider apostolic way of speaking about life in Christ.

Paul argues that love fulfils the law, summing up the commandments in one word. It supports the elder's claim that the many commandments of verse 6 are gathered into the one commandment to walk in love.

The psalmist asks to be taught God's way so that he may walk in His truth. It shows that the elder's phrase has deep Old Testament roots, and that walking in the truth was always a matter of God teaching and of the heart being united to fear Him.

Israel is asked to fear the LORD, to walk in all His ways, to love Him and to serve Him with all the heart. The verse joins walking, loving and obeying in one sentence, as verse 6 does, and shows that the pairing of love and obedience is as old as the covenant.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture can be told as a story of walking. In Eden the man and his wife heard the LORD God walking in the garden, Genesis 3:8, and humanity was meant to walk with Him. Sin broke the fellowship and drove the pair out of the garden, but God did not stop calling people to the walk. Enoch walked with God, Genesis 5:24, Noah walked with God, Genesis 6:9, and God told Abram to walk before Him and be blameless, Genesis 17:1. When He redeemed Israel, He gave a Law that was to shape a walk: walk in all His ways, love Him, serve Him, Deuteronomy 10:12.

The story of Israel is then a story of a people who could not keep the walk. The prophets accused them of going their own way, and the exile was the end of a long failure to love and obey. But the prophets also looked ahead. God would give a new covenant, writing His law on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33, and would put His Spirit within His people and cause them to walk in His statutes, Ezekiel 36:27.

The elder's paragraph belongs to the fulfilment of those promises. The Son came and kept the Father's commandments perfectly, John 15:10, and He died to deal with the failure that had made the walk impossible. By His Spirit He now enables those who trust Him to walk in the way that Israel could not, so that the righteous standard of the law is fulfilled in them, Romans 8:4. The little household of 2 John, with its children walking in the truth, is a small piece of that promise come true.

The story is still moving. The elder's love commandment is given to a church that still lives among deceivers and false paths, and the walking is not yet effortless. But it is leading somewhere. In the new creation the nations will walk by the light of the city, Revelation 21:24, and the walk with God that began in the garden will be restored with nothing in the way. Love will no longer need to be commanded, because it will be the air of the place, and the path that begins with a household in the truth will end in the presence of the God who has walked among His people from the start.

sermon.title: Response, Request, Reminder
sermon.why: Begg preaches this passage, 2 John 1:4-6, tracing the elder's joy over children walking in the truth, his request that they love one another, and the reminder that love means walking in obedience. A clear, orthodox treatment of this movement.

quiz.q: What made the elder overjoyed in verse 4?

options.text: He found some of the lady's children walking in the truth.
options.note: Verse 4 names his joy: children living by the truth, as the Father commanded.

options.text: The children had grown wealthy and successful.
options.note: His joy is over faithfulness to the truth, not worldly success.

options.text: The false teachers had finally been silenced.
options.note: That would be welcome, but the stated cause of joy is the children walking in truth, not the silencing of opponents.

options.text: The children had invented a new teaching.
options.note: The elder prizes the old command, not novelty; new teaching is the danger, not the joy.

quiz.q: How does the elder describe the commandment to love one another?

options.text: Not a new commandment, but one they have had from the beginning.
options.note: Verse 5 stresses the command is old and familiar, not an innovation.

options.text: A brand new rule he is introducing for the first time.
options.note: He expressly says it is not new but from the beginning.

options.text: An optional ideal for the especially mature.
options.note: It is a commandment for all, not an optional extra.

options.text: A hard saying that few could be expected to keep.
options.note: It is demanding, but the elder presents it as the familiar, binding path for all believers, not an impossible ideal.

options.text: That we walk according to God's commandments.
options.note: Verse 6 defines love as obedient walking, and the commandment as walking in love.

options.text: A warm feeling toward other people.
options.note: Love here is defined by obedient action, not mainly by feeling.

options.text: Tolerating whatever others choose to believe.
options.note: The letter ties love to truth and obedience, not to indifference about belief.

options.text: Doing kind acts whenever it is convenient.
options.note: Love does show in action, but verse 6 grounds it in walking according to God's commandments, not mere convenience.

quiz.q: How are love and obedience related in this passage?

options.text: They define each other: love is keeping God's commandments, and His commandment is to love.
options.note: The two are bound together, each interpreting the other.

options.text: Obedience matters, but love is a separate and higher thing.
options.note: Love is central, but the passage will not separate it from obedience; it defines love by it.

options.text: Love replaces obedience, so commandments no longer matter.
options.note: The opposite; love is defined as walking according to His commandments.

options.text: They have nothing to do with each other.
options.note: The passage locks them together deliberately.

questions: The elder was overjoyed to see believers walking in the truth. Whose faithfulness has recently brought you joy, and have you told them?
Love here is not a mere feeling but a way of walking, obeying God day by day. Where is God calling you to show love this week in concrete obedience rather than warm words alone?
The command to love one another is old, from the beginning, yet always needs renewing. In what relationship has your love cooled, and what would it look like to take up the old command afresh?
This letter refuses to split love from truth or love from obedience. Are you tempted to keep one without the others, and how might holding all three together change the way you treat people?

translationNotes.note: 'Some of your children' need not imply the rest were unfaithful; it likely reflects that the elder had met only some of them, and rejoiced at what he saw.
The Greek weaves love and commandment together tightly: love is defined as walking in the commandments, and the commandment is to walk in love, a deliberate circle binding the two.
